full_text:
Interviewer:	Ok how long have you been here for then.

Subject:	Since July the 5th which would be 7 months now.

Interviewer:	You’ve been here all the time? 

Subject:	Yeah. 

Interviewer:	OK, can you tell me a bit about [company] and what they do?

Subject:	Well, basically they’re quite a big company. They do specialise in civils although they do other bits and pieces like building and things like that. Erm, probably their best things are water they do a lot of sewage works and roads and er this project is a road by pass around between [town] and [town] across the (?) Valley. And that's a 34 million project I think and it's a design board and should finish it April 2006.

Interviewer:	Most of the roads seemed quite good round here, like dual carriage way and stuff.

Subject:	Yeah I mean there's a lot of work going on in [area] and we’ve got quite a bit of it. Er we've got another job starting in up in the valleys in April. And we've got quite a lot of M1 junction jobs we've just finished [place] obviously that's quite a big job. Er yeah there's quite a lot going on actually it's looking good.

Interviewer:	OK, how would you describe the company’s attitude to women?

Subject:	Erm very good, extremely good very erm, erm I wouldn’t say, I wouldn’t, no I haven’t been treated any differently to any of the guys I know. I mean there's not many women here, there's me, there's [name] who is doing industrial placement as well from [town] and there's erm 2 girls who have graduated and they’re in their early, mid 20’s and they’re both engineers. But they’re the only ones on site, but there's no discrimination for or against I’d say really.

Interviewer:	OK I’ll ask some more questions about that later then.

Subject:	OK

Interviewer:	How useful do you think that your course has been so far to the work that you're doing?

Subject:	Er useful – zero I’d say erm because all I've learnt is levelling. I learnt surveying and the other thing I've - that's about it really, I haven’t used anything from uni here. (OK) But I think that's probably, everyone else has found that as well I think.

Interviewer:	Yeah do you think that's, do you think that matters?

Subject:	Erm I wish, I wish it was a bit more practical, the degree, but I think coming out on site. The degree is trying teach me to design as well as prac as well being on site practically and stuff like that and er erm being at site has probably you get that anyway if you know what I mean. You don’t need a degree for it…

Interviewer:	It's just something that you need to go out and do?

Subject:	I think if it was now and I was 18 without a degree I probably would have gained the same amount of knowledge but erm it's weird how you need a degree to do things you're not, you know what I mean? It's hard to explain really.

Interviewer:	Do you think that you’ve used like generic skills from uni?

Subject:	From uni? Well I've learnt well things like organisation and yeah and management stuff like that, working in teams and things like that. That's been good but a lot of it has been your own personality, you’ve got to have common sense, you’ve got to be organised in yourself. You have to be able to talk to people, things like that really.

Interviewer:	Is there anything then that you wish that you had learnt then at uni, before you started?

Subject:	Erm, just I think knowing names of things that everyone knows out on site, like I want to know more about piling and standard operations that go on you know, that everyone seems to know about but you don’t because you haven’t learnt it and it's not it's not really relevant in the degree that's the only thing – not knowing the names of things really.

Interviewer:	Yeah but do you think that is something that could be taught, do you think?

Subject:	Yeah I think if we had more site visits that would be helpful.

Interviewer:	Did you have any site visits?

Subject:	No none. I went on one but that was with an external group that was with the Civil Engineering Society so. It would be really helpful if we did that more.

Interviewer:	OK did uni teach you anything about Health & Safety?

Subject:	Erm there’s a small, there's module in the first year but that was mostly about lab and stuff most of what I've learnt about Health & Safety has probably been from being out on site last summer and this year again.

Interviewer:	Have you had to do lots of Health & Safety training here?

Subject:	I have done a day course and I do, there's been loads of talks here we've done quite a lot of stuff in house within this area. And a lot of it you just learn out on site and from the other engineers and when you write method statements and things and from like my boss and things like that – just what you pick up.

Interviewer:	Would it be useful to have more of that at uni or is it something that…

Subject:	Yes but there's so much, I think it's probably best to leave it out on the site thing because there's so much and it's all so specific and if you go into it and I mean there are general things but like scaffolding. There's just so many different areas and I think it's best to leave it to site because you don’t really understand it until you’ve been out on site anyway. (Yeah) Yeah.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think then that uni could do more to prepare you for going to work or the placement?

Subject:	Well it was such a shock but I don’t think they could have done anything about it because I said that at the beginning actually. Like there wasn’t much help involved for like moving, I was moving house and I didn’t have a clue what I was doing. I mean to a new area.

Interviewer:	It’s quite scary that isn’t it? 

Subject:	It was. I was to tell you the truth the first few months were really, really hard because I didn’t know anyone but it's something that some people stayed at home. Some people have moved a half an hour down the road, and some people have you know it's some people went to offices and people have gone into sewage works. It's such a varied thing there's no way you could teach, teach it all to one class because some, well no one would listen because it's not relevant to half of them.

Interviewer:	Did you have a choice of sites or did you just get put here?

Subject:	No I got put here erm which first was like that’s really far away and erm but erm I didn’t really mind where I was going to go but now I’m quite glad I’m here.

Interviewer:	How useful do you think it was doing a summer placement?

Subject:	Er it helped me out quite a lot with knowing bits and pieces about the company. Knowing erm like bits of health and safety I knew, that was quite helpful.

Interviewer:	Are you doing similar work or is it totally different?

Subject:	Oh, it's totally different I was erm a secretary basically in the summer for – it wasn’t really it was our site but we sub-contracted everything to the sub contractor. Whereas here [company] are the contractor. We've got about 4 or 5 general subcontractors but we do all the engineering if you know what I mean? And here I've got my own section, I've got like stuff that I need to do that no-one else can do if you know what I mean? Which makes me feel responsible so it's quite good.

Interviewer:	Yeah okay, what you said about moving was quite a big issue, but how have you found the sort of transition from education to work apart from that?

Subject:	Oh I love it working – I like the erm I don’t mind the hours I mean I get up at 6 every day. It was hard at the beginning, the first month I was tired constantly and I wasn’t used to like constantly running round all day and then getting home at 7 and collapsing. Erm you know there's, there's good and bad to each one really isn’t there? I mean at uni I found myself, you get lazy don’t you really just like hanging around but erm I really enjoy it and I think I've done it quite well. Some people have really I mean my housemate [name] works for [company] and he can't get up in the morning. He’s terrible and he’s always late but I’m, no I don’t mind it at all, it definitely suits me I think.

Interviewer:	Are you looking forward to going back to uni then?

Subject:	I am as well yeah I am quite looking forward to it because I really like, it's not that I'm not exercising my brain here, but I really like doing the projects and things that you do at uni and I’m quite looking forward to doing my final year project and stuff like that.

Interviewer:	Do you think you’ll use what you’ve learnt here when you're in your final year?

Subject:	Oh yeah so much. I'm thinking about doing - you know we've got to do a erm 4000 word report for our dissertation er our DIS. I am doing that on noise and vibration which I'm doing a lot of monitoring on and I'm thinking about doing that for my final year project as well but yeah they’ve really helped me out.

Interviewer:	Do you feel like you’ve had to face any new issues with work?

Subject:	Well as I say like when I got here they said right you can do the monitoring and they threw these, well they didn’t throw them at me, but basically they said here you go you can go out and you know monitor the noise and vibration. And, I was like HELP, so I sort of tried to teach myself and it's a slow process really of and I ended up going up to [town] to see these people who actually made these machines and they got me they taught me how to use them. and, now I'm like, I wouldn’t say I was an expert on them, but I know what they mean and how to use them and so it’s quite sad but on site I am the actual expert, 21 year old an industrial placement student and that's and that's something I'm quite proud of really. It sounds a bit sad but it's erm it's gotten kind of a big issue with a lot of residents around and there's a lot of noise going on and there's a lot of vibration with track machines and rollers and things and you just need to make sure we’re not violating the contract with the council and things like that. So, that's quite a big issue I've had to put up with, as well as things like erm I’m looking at er resister and retaining walls and when I first started I didn’t have a clue about when to get like materials in, erm I didn’t know what I needed to do brickwork and things like that and that's just something I just can reel off now. I'm just you know what I mean? That's it's just things you get used to and stuff like that, yeah its good.

Interviewer:	I was going to ask you a bit about responsibility but I’ll ask you that in a minute. Apart from the technical stuff, do you think you’ve had to learn new stuff, like how to deal with different people and..

Subject:	There's a lot of politics involved and I wasn’t ready for that.

Interviewer:	Was that difficult getting used to?

Subject:	Yeah it was hard getting used to it. I know it's probably like that in every workplace but erm it's hard to - I'm very like obviously it's like I'm used to hanging out with my peers and things like even when I was at work I was just like you know but here you’ve got to be you know you’ve got to speak to a manager in a certain way and respect them. And listen to them and things like that and that's something I've got used to and try not to. Also writing stuff in emails is difficult, it was just something really small, but ...

Interviewer:	I’ve had that problem in my first job.

Subject:	Did you? Like my ‘I’s and my yeah and my writing in MSM language and I've got to go back through it - so that's been – which is interesting really.

Interviewer:	Well my thing was (laughter) - I sent an email to somebody in my previous job I was sending an email to someone, I can't remember but I think it would have been okay and the person I was actually sending it to I'm sure didn’t bat an eyelid, but I had copied my boss into it. (Uh oh) And he told me I shouldn’t have written an email like that or worded like that to that person.

Subject:	Was it really …

Interviewer:	Well it wasn’t that casual but I think it was because I worked for Local Government and it was - I think he was probably more bothered about the office politics than the guy that I was actually sending it to (inaudible) and there weren’t any other repercussions apart from that. So I think if I hadn’t copied my boss into it, it would have been fine but …

Subject:	But that's the thing I've learnt as well you’ve got to tell like – the council wants to know like certain results from monitoring and so I’ll just tell them and then the Project Manager says to me, you know I need to know everything that goes to the council and I'm just like ‘okay’.

Interviewer:	And it's like they need to know that information but you have to dress it up in a certain way.

Subject:	Yeah it's just it's interesting things that I've picked up and because I'm in now the monitoring position I'm in, I'm I've got to like explain things to people who don’t know what I'm talking about and that's really difficult. I'm not very good at explaining things like I'm just like oh you know what I mean, and I'm having to like break it down and not kind of like patronise people but I'm finding that hard because I'm not used to that like probably because in engineering you don’t write stuff, you just do stuff, know what I mean?

Interviewer:	Yeah, (laughter), do you think that uni could be structured differently to reflect more what it's like in industry? Or do you think they’re just totally separate?

Subject:	I think well the reason it's like that isn’t it, is because of the ICE isn’t it? Because they say we have to do this amount of mass, this amount of structures and all that stuff. Erm, I don’t want to put down my lecturers but I wish they were more practical and had been around site more recently than 20 years ago do you know what I mean?

Interviewer:	Yeah so maybe more up-to-date with current affairs and things like that?

Subject:	Yeah it's I was saying actually to my friend the other day how it might be good to split the degree up into people want to be out on site and people who want to be in the office but it's hard to say. Maybe keep the first year the same and then maybe split up in the second year and say right you want to be out on site and you want to do surveying and ordering in materials and knowing about all of this stuff and you can be in the design office and know about calculations and concrete and everything like that, and that sounds like an ideal word and I think it sounds like a really good idea really.

Interviewer:	Having more optional modules?

Subject:	Yeah exactly.

Interviewer:	But the thing at the minute is whether you can still get the accreditation?

Subject:	Yeah exactly do I still have the same like as a well would I still have the same level as somebody who has done design but then it means I’m stuck in the site industry, but then again you find a lot of people won't go into an office and I've got like, my engineering friends they’re like in their 28’s, 29’s and they don’t want to go into an office ever. People just aren’t office people sometimes you know. That's just, that’s quite a good idea actually I might ring up the ICE and say yeah what do you think?

Interviewer:	OK do you think then that work and uni have different priorities and goals?

Subject:	Hmm they have still got the deadline thing, which is in both but I at uni I'm kind of like not left my, here I’m left to my own devices in the fact that I'm given like my boss said can you do this for me? And I’ll say that I’ll do it in the next couple of days but I've got other things that I need to do and you’ve got to prioritise. I suppose that’s the same kind of thing, say at uni you’ve got a deadline the next day you've got to do that first - the same kind of thing really but at work you’ll find that someone will ring you up and say I've got a crisis you need to come out now and then you're stuck because you’ve got to do this thing that has to be done by the next day. So, I would say at work it's more planning your time and being aware of being ready for like something to like come up do you know what I mean. I'm sorry…

Interviewer:	Yes no it's all right. Do you think the work that you're doing at work it's not just for yourself either?

Subject:	Oh no.

Interviewer:	Even though you’re working by yourself.

Subject:	You always help each other out.

Interviewer:	But you’ve got a responsibility to the company.

Subject:	Yeah exactly but we’re, in our office, we’re quite a big team and we’re all like if someone needs a hand you go out and you help them out. Or you say to them well I can't do it now but I can do it tomorrow morning and they go, okay then. And erm you just try and work around each other if you need a hand and that's quite good.

Interviewer:	OK do [company] have a structure or programme in place for placement students?

Subject:	Yes they’ve got quite a big graduate programme. Erm and like the other day the Chief Engineer was talking to me about getting chartered. With industrial placement students they’re kind of like if they introduce the ideas then they put them on courses and you kind of, they make you think, [company] is quite a good company I would like to work for them when I leave. And they have invested quite a lot in you so they wouldn’t say no if you said you know I want to work for [company], do you know what I mean? So, I mean I've been put in like 3 courses so far and I've got another one coming up in March and I’m going to work for them when I leave definitely because I think they're a good company. I know the structure of them, it's easy because I know several people who work for here and stuff. So, and there is a good programme, they try and get you chartered straightaway, they try and get you interested in it when you're like 22. So, that you're not being at 28 and oh I wish I got chartered. Hmm so yeah good programme but then again I think quite a lot of the big companies do so …

Interviewer:	So you're sponsored aren’t you?

Subject:	I was, but erm I am now on the BEng so, but I did speak to my erm the guy who sponsors me and he said if you do a good job this year then we’ll sponsor you in your final year and just work for us when you leave.

Interviewer:	That's good then.

Subject:	So that's quite good yeah.

Interviewer:	You’ve told me about your role a bit, is there anything else?

Subject:	Not really those are the 2 main things really I think.

Interviewer:	Are the things that you're doing what you expected you would be doing or what you were told to expect?

Subject:	Hmm I think, I think I kind of expected I would be like kind of chain girl, helping out other people. Like helping out the other engineers who needed a hand. I didn’t expect I’d have all this responsibility on my own and I've really although at the beginning I was so scared. I am now really enjoying it and I've actually got my own wall starting up in a couple of weeks as well so that's quite exciting. I've got loads of people around to help me out with it but it's at the end of the day it's my responsibility.

Interviewer:	So you feel like that you’ve been given the right amount of responsibility? It's snowing.

Subject:	Yeah, yeah oooh wow that's cool isn’t it?

Interviewer:	No, I've got to drive home.

Subject:	Oh it's all right (inaudible).

Interviewer:	So even though you’ve got responsibility, you feel like there are people are around you to support you?

Subject:	Oh yeah definitely I mean at the beginning I thought I would be thrown in at the deep end but that's always the best way to do it – it really is because it makes you – instead of like throwing you in gently it's really the best way to do it I think.

Interviewer:	OK how would you summarise your placement experience so far then?

Subject:	I would say it's the most useful thing I've done in uni. Definitely erm I would say it's being challenging, er it's not just being the work it's being the fact I've been – again I've moved away from anyone I've known. I've been left on my own, I was living in the house that I'm living in for 3 months on my own and it has just made me realise – I thought I was really independent and responsible and all of this stuff and I was so, so not. I was ringing my parents everyday going (inaudible) and the only thing I’d do is go to work really early and stay for ages because I didn’t want to leave and I think it's just been, made me realise how erm I can do it now I'm in on my own. And I have so many friends who are just living at home and they’re just like – I don’t know how you're doing it Amy and I'm just like, well. I'm quite proud of myself really do you know.

Interviewer:	Do you think that you’ve changed?

Subject:	Oh yes I've grown up quite a lot I think and er thinking about my future more as well and what I want to do with my life – I wasn’t that bothered about that last year.

Interviewer:	Do you think that the fact that you’ve had to go off and do all these things alone will help you loads?

Subject:	Yeah I really do because it's going to be like this when I'm at work if I work for [company] it will be like this when I'm older definitely.

Interviewer:	Yeah if you come and work for them will they be just able to say we want you here, here or here?

Subject:	Yeah basically that's what it will be like they’ll say I want you here and you’ll be there for approximately 2 years and you’ll be like okay right find somewhere to live, move somewhere I don’t know, have no friends, start all over again you know.

Interviewer:	Yeah that doesn’t bother you at all then?

Subject:	Erm not really not at the moment but I can see myself in 5 years being bothered by it as most people are to be honest erm you’ve got like – my friend [name] she has just bought a house in [town], which is about 15 minutes south of here.

Interviewer:	Yeah that's where ...

Subject:	She’s got a base at the moment but she’s going to be moving up and wherever you don’t know where’s she’s going to be in the next few years and it's quite a hassle. Erm yeah but you know at the moment it's not too bad – see how it goes eh?

Interviewer:	What would you say had been the best and worst things about placement so far?

Subject:	Hmm worse thing – pressure that I've had with certain things like monitors broke down both of them and I had I didn’t know how to fix them. I’d send them away and then it's the day we've got the loudest thing going on and all this hassle from the residents, the council and I was just like, oh my God I'm going to explode and erm that was hard. But that you know it passed but that was a really hard week. The best thing has probably been reactions from people like how – I talk to residents on site I go out quite a lot and they're like so kind and there's like some of the residents are really nice and really friendly to you. And some of them are really horrible but people are really nice and I just like meeting all of the different people like you’ve got site people, you’ve got labourers, you’ve got, I quite like that. I might be a Community Liaisons Officer I don’t know, that's an option yeah. I got five out of five for team work as well so I was quite impressed with that. (Well done) Because we had a performance review about a month ago, so.

Interviewer:	Does everyone have that or is that part of the placement?

Subject:	Hmm it's everyone, everyone had it and I didn’t think we needed it because we’re only contracted to, because apparently they're for pay rises and we’re only contracted to what we get so I didn’t think there was any point in me doing it but we did it anyway. It was quite useful actually I had a chat with [name] about it, he's my Section Manger, so it was quite nice.

Interviewer:	Yeah do you think that there are any drawbacks to getting a placement or is it all positive things?

Subject:	No, no drawbacks at all. I don’t care what people say about this one year thing, it's pathetic.

Interviewer:	You would definitely recommend other people to do it then?

Subject:	If you're a bit older and you're really bothered about being held back one year then fair enough but if you're say under 25 then do it.

Interviewer:	Do you think it's been an advantage or a disadvantage having another placement student there?

Subject:	I would say a non vantage because there's no other placement students in my section. There's 2 in road works and I don’t really - it's not that I don't talk to them but I mean I have give one of them a lift to work every day but they're in completely different section to me and both at [name] Uni so I don’t really have anything in common with them. I mean we've been out a couple of times but what are you talking about work wise or friends wise or just?

Interviewer:	Well just like whether you support each other?

Subject:	No not really because were in a different section.

Interviewer:	It's not an advantage or disadvantage?

Subject:	No it's not really an issue. I mean if they was other placement students in my area I think it would be disadvantage to be honest, because I’d probably be, we’d probably be paired up and probably have to split everything, do you know what I mean. So, I probably think it's maybe a disadvantage.

Interviewer:	OK that's fine.

Subject:	They don’t see me, they don’t oh you're an industrial placed student they just see me as a…

Interviewer:	That was my next question.

Subject:	Carry on.

Interviewer:	It's okay (laughter) I was just going to say do you feel like you are treated like a placement student or do you feel like a normal member of staff.

Subject:	I'm just a normal member of staff and they call you engineers as a group so I’m just you know I mean I do the everything the same as everyone else. I write diaries, I use the (?) all the time. You do over time if I want to, you know, so there's no difference at all, I mean apart from they get paid more than I do.

Interviewer:	OK do you have to do a lot of group work?

Subject:	No you do there's pair work like I’ll go out with [name] or something and help him out with if it needs like, me telling the staff or something like that and then I’ll do the same to him if I need I hand, but erm I would say we don’t go out as a group because we all everyone has different structures and everyone has different areas to work in. So, no it doesn’t really happen to be honest.

Interviewer:	OK do you think though that doing at team work at uni is worthwhile?

Subject:	Yeah, yeah.

Interviewer:	And does that help you when you go to work?

Subject:	You have to work with people you don’t like in real life so you know. There are a couple of people around here that some people don’t like and some we don’t get on with and find a bit overbearing but you’ve still you know got to work with them. Especially if they're your boss or your manager, so yeah it's a good idea. I think it's more for people into design office though because of the way they do it there's a lot of design work in groups and that's how they do it in the design offices I think so.

Interviewer:	OK have you get a mentor at all?

Subject:	Well there's [name] my Section Manager, he's really great and he’ll, I can speak to him if I've got any problems but to be honest, all the engineers are great.

Interviewer:	Yes so there's lots of people like you can go to for advice?

Subject:	Yeah definitely.

Interviewer:	OK is there anyone that you’d regard as like a role model at all?

Subject:	Yeah the other girls, 2 other girls that we've got, [name] who is 23, she has just bought a house. She is really clever and I just want to, she’s got her own bridge and she’s only 23 and I think that's really, really, cool and she’s (inaudible) she was working at [town] as well and that's cool I think. I would like to be like her and there's [name] as well she’s got erm have you seen the big bridge when you came over?

Interviewer:	Probably.

Subject:	Er there's a picture of it out there I’ll show you it's amazing and she's working as part of that and that's called, that's PDS that's an amazing structure that's going to be like the whole landmark for this whole place- it's huge. Take a look when you go back.

Interviewer:	Have you had anyone from uni come to visit you?

Subject:	Yeah I did, some guy came to see me in November, I don’t know his name.

Interviewer:	So it wasn’t anyone you knew?

Subject:	No I think he was a new guy he was like he was an engineer and he was erm a I don’t know a GEO Tech guy from the department I think he had just joined. I wish they would send someone I knew you know that would have been so much better… next question.

Interviewer:	Do you think it would have helped if it was?

Subject:	Yeah.

Interviewer:	Made it easier?

Subject:	I mean he was a nice guy but erm it wasn’t really like, he just said, how are you doing? I said fine and he goes what are have you got any thoughts on what you're doing for your final year project? And I was like some thoughts. Just a bit of a chat not really, he didn’t seem that bothered to be honest, not that I'm having a go at him. I mean sure he’d seen like 3 other people that day so but erm if I had any problems I would probably speak to [placement coordinator] instead but I haven’t really so ...

Interviewer:	Do you think it's a good idea that you have someone come to see you then?

Subject:	Yeah certainly I do you feel because I mean especially I do I feel really disconnected out here. I can't access my email well I can access them but I can't email back and I would really like to talk to someone about my final year project but I can't because I can't email anyone back. If I try and ring anyone there's never anyone in and I try ringing other people as well like area people like to talk about noise and stuff and there's no one in so I was just like – you do feel disconnected. And even when you go up to uni it's like oh it's really weird I don’t recognise anyone, everyone’s really young. So yes it's definitely a good idea. Bit of tangent there sorry.

Interviewer:	That's fine. If you had any problems out on placement then who would you talk to about that?

Subject:	It depends on what types of problems they were I think if it's like with the work I would speak to [name] and if it was like it depends really because if I would probably talk about it to [name] with anything. Because [placement coordinator] can't really help me because he’s too far away and I don’t want to leave this place. If it's something like that I would probably talk to [name] definitely.

Interviewer:	OK do you know if either uni or here have got a complaints procedure if you did have any problems?

Subject:	I know there's a complaints procedure for uni definitely erm you’ve got to go through [placement coordinator] and then he goes through higher up people or something. Erm here – I'm sure they do but I wouldn’t know about it.

Interviewer:	That's all right. Are there appropriate facilities for women here?

Subject:	 [Name] said you’d say that, [name] said you better ask Samantha because she is on a site yeah?
